design: Riders: tree calculus that reads without consuming. The loaded program (leaf, stem, fork) never changes and is never copied. Each application is a frame with two riders. A rider is a pointer that sits on a wire and walks down the code it reads. Finished frames become the stem or fork they built, or a receipt that keeps the argument K or a leaf triage dropped. History is the frames, the riders, receipts left on the code's wires, and one thread mark per rider move. Forget is the only irreversible rule. I checked it against its own abstract model (/tmp/riders/sim.py) with added instruments: per-wire record piles, one reader per node per round, and garbage buried under later work. Larger inputs were added: add n 1 for n up to 64, and fib 3 to 8. The comparison is the repo's lazy-net tool (research/linear-nets/target/release/linear-nets). I also re-fetched the citations that carry weight.
fatal_flaws: Sharing code without copies makes every computation that uses a node share that node's history, so exact undo without ids conflicts with local unwinding. Riders and records on a code wire are ordered: a rider must be the lowest item to read, T4 puts receipts on top, and T1/T2 riders stay at the bottom. So the order in which unrelated computations used a node is part of the history. The design records it with a pass count and an 'M1' thread mark, but neither says what was passed. Counterexample: the wire above X reads [b, a, X], with a's count k+1 and top mark M1. Past 1: a passed b. Past 2: a passed a rider c; c passed a back and read X; then a K receipt b and its rider landed on top, and the rider passed a and read X. In both pasts a's reverse M1 is enabled. In past 2 it lifts a above b, which arrived later. That is two pasts for one state, Bennett's merge. The NICT abstract the design cites predicts exactly this: reordering signal arrivals can destroy the reversibility of a circuit built from reversible parts. Every repair costs a premise. (1) Forbid passing, so each wire is a strict stack. Then records come off last-in-first-out, and a dropped computation can unwind only after every later use of the same code unwinds. In the model, 28-36% of the garbage records in fib 4-8 sit under later needed records (0-19% on the other calls). rev.rs (the event-log engine) undoes independent events in any order. Cleaning up one call also cannot run while other calls of the same code keep running. (2) Let records swap freely. Then their order is entropy, and taking one off a k-deep wire costs about kT ln k, so unwinding is no longer free. (3) Record who passed whom: that is ids. CCSK, cited as precedent, works only because unique communication keys pair the two sides of each step. The only escape that keeps the other premises is giving each use its own copy of the code (bud), which makes its history private. That is the duplicator again.

'Copies are never needed for parallelism in time' is false under the design's own exclusion rule. 'R over X' means the lowest item on X's wire, so a code node serves one reader at a time. That makes each node a serial module, and by Keller's Theorem 3.1 (cited by the design against token machines) no set of serial modules can build a parallel one. So k concurrent callers of one function take at least k steps at each shared node. A frame parked in tr over a triage's arms, waiting for its argument, either blocks every later caller (no passing) or swaps back and forth with them (passing, with counts and marks growing while they wait). Riders are ordered and exclusive, like hard-core particles, not bosons. Geometry of Synthesis, also cited, shares a circuit only where its type system rules out overlapping uses: contraction is allowed in products, not in application. The fix the design offers, bud, is the duplicator. The measured cost is small at this benchmark's concurrency: with one reader per node per round, rounds rise 0-8% (fib 8 +1%), since at most 16 frames ever want one node in a round. So this breaks the claim and criterion 2 at hot code, not the current numbers. A wide workload, with many calls of one function at once, pays time proportional to the number of callers at each shared node unless it buds.

Criterion 7 is not met for disp programs. Compiled code leaves receipts: add 2 3 leaves 154, or 51 with labels. Nothing in the core lets a tree-calculus program read, consume or reuse a receipt. The history-free add needs new frame modes, riders that move up, and bead rules written in the substrate, installed as a label: that is a jet. The only generic way to clear history is Bennett's copy-out and run-back, which keeps the whole run's history until the end. Meeting criterion 7 needs a two-way primitive in disp itself, for example running a function backward on its result plus its receipt. The design does not propose one.

fixable_flaws.flaw: As specified, records sit in the read path, so recursion is quadratic and the headline numbers do not hold. T1/T2 riders stay over code leaves and stems, K and leaf-triage receipts go on code wires, and every later reader must pass them all to become the lowest item. The model never charges this. I added it as a lower bound: one pass per record per read, without counting a K's own receipt. add n 1 piles 2n+2 records on one code leaf: one K receipt and one T1 rider per loop iteration. Passes are 9.3x the steps at add 64 1 and 11x at fib 8. Compared with the lazy net (today's tree-calculus net run lazily), the 21 benchmark calls' geometric means move from 0.17x work and 0.52x depth to 0.31x and 0.74x. Against the net with movement agents they move from 0.32x and 1.01x to 0.59x and 1.42x, which fails Step 1's own depth bar of 1.15x. At add 64 1 Riders does 2.05x the lazy net's work at 2.84x its depth; at fib 8, 1.80x and 4.85x. Depth already loses at add 16 1 and fib 5.
fixable_flaws.fix: Keep pure records off the read path: give each code wire one anchor agent with a side pile the records stack on, so a reader passes only the anchor. Let each rider remember the shape of the persistent node it points at, so leaf reads and shape tests never have to reach the node. Give a T2 fork a direct rider on the stem's child (one blank) instead of reaching it through the T2 record. Keep live pointers to one node in a balanced sharing tree: about log k passes per read, and in 3D about the cube root of k sites away. Re-measure on add n 1 up to n = 64 and fib up to 8, not only calls.txt.

fixable_flaws.flaw: The abstract model is not the design. It has no order on wires and no exclusion: any number of frames read a node in the same round. It charges no passes over records. T2 builds a fresh fork with direct children, while the design's fork-frame reaches its left child through its function rider and the stem; 16-19% of all steps read such a left child. It puts zero distance between a frame's function code and its argument. It recomputes demand from the root every round, so dropped work stops instantly. The repo's 'holders' run grew add 1 1 to 8x the agents when work inside kept arguments went on. Every work, depth and history ratio inherits these gaps.
fixable_flaws.fix: Before Step 1, extend the model with per-wire stacks and one reader per node per round, two-hop forks, a distance charge per triage, and demand withdrawal as a pulse with latency. The last is cheap to settle: a 10-round withdrawal latency costs +9% steps on 16-bit relay_add and nothing on fib or add.

fixable_flaws.flaw: Pass bookkeeping is unbounded. Pass counts are per-rider integers, so the agents are not finite-state. 'Every rule that moves a rider pushes a mark' includes M1, so marks grow with passes: about 103,000 pass marks against 13,274 step marks at add 64 1, and about 318,000 against 34,498 at fib 8. That makes the history 5.5-6.4x the model's count. If rev.rs keeps its fib 2 to fib 3 growth, this passes the 'at most a fifth of rev.rs' bar by fib 5-6. Two riders on one wire, each 'not yet over its value' while their frames wait, keep passing each other and pushing marks for as long as they wait.
fixable_flaws.fix: No rider passes another rider: riders read in arrival order. With side piles there is nothing else to pass, so the count and the M1 marks disappear. A rider enters a code wire only when its frame can fire on arrival.

fixable_flaws.flaw: T4, T5 and T9 move or create a rider on F.right while their own rider sits at the bottom of F.left's wire. So the parent fork F, every rider queued on F.left and the node under it must fit in one 2x2x2 block. A second caller of the same function, or a frame parked in tr waiting for its argument, sits between F and that rider. Past a block's capacity the rule cannot fire, and with M1 the riders swap back and forth instead. The stall comes exactly under the sharing the design is built for.
fixable_flaws.fix: Fire T3+T4, T3+T5 and T3+T6+T7/8/9 as one step from F's own wire, using shape labels set at load time. K and Sx labels already exist; add one for triage. Then no rule needs F and a rider deep inside F.left together. Frames that wait for an argument still hold F's wire; see the parallelism flaw.

fixable_flaws.flaw: Frames are not local. T7-T9 read the node under R_a (argument data) and move R_f (at the function's code) in the same rule. A T2 fork's left child is two hops away, through another frame's thread. The 'two halves exchanging pulses' the text relies on are not in the agent or rule list. On the lattice, every triage and every two-hop read costs the distance from code to data. The design itself quotes reads at 9-64 sites from where code was loaded. None of this is in the step or round counts.
fixable_flaws.fix: Make a frame two agents, a function half at the code and an argument half at the data, joined by a wire. Write the pulse rules and their reverses, and charge the distance in the model.

fixable_flaws.flaw: Reverse rules do not check for readers. Reading leaves no trace on the value read, so a stem-frame can run T1 backward to app while a rider that moved into its child still depends on it. The backward run then reaches states no forward run reaches. Step 1's check that 'exactly one rule's reverse applies' is also ill-posed with many frames, since many reverses always apply.
fixable_flaws.fix: Have every rider that moves through a value leave a mark there, cleared when it comes back, and allow that value's reverse only when no marks are left. Count the marks as history. Check instead that the enabled reverses are exactly the latest event of each chain of causes.

fixable_flaws.flaw: The physical claims do not follow. Bijective rules plus 'identity elsewhere' do not make a permutation of block states. A right-hand side that is not also a left-hand side collides with the identity. Overlapping rule instances in one block need a fixed order. A deterministic version needs a direction bit or momentum per frame. Metropolis with a demand bias is a random process, not a block unitary, so the Schumacher-Werner reading covers only a deterministic version, which is not specified. The demand drive costs heat on every forward step, passes included, so heat is quadratic as specified. That contradicts 'heat is paid only by forget'.
fixable_flaws.fix: Write the deterministic block rule with a direction bit (or demon energy) per frame. Check by enumeration that it permutes block states. Put drive heat and any ordering entropy in the heat ledger.

fixable_flaws.flaw: Forget corrupts other riders' history. Removing a receipt from the middle of a wire leaves every rider that passed it with an M1 mark that now refers to a different neighbour, so their reverses go wrong.
fixable_flaws.fix: Side piles, so nothing ever passes a record. Forget only from the top of a pile, or splice inside a pile where no one's record refers to positions.

fixable_flaws.flaw: Several citations are used against what they say. HVM2's REF expansion copies the whole definition at every call ('The definition is essentially copied from the static Book'), the opposite of code read in place. CCSK keeps history in the process structure only because unique keys pair the two sides of each step: exactly the ids Riders gives up. In Dal Lago et al. (arXiv 1405.3427) tokens are positions that never occupy an edge, so 'tokens do not interact' does not carry over to riders, which queue and pass. Jaynes is cited for 'dropping a reference costs nothing', but the design's own heat table prices a dropped pointer into code at log2 of the places it could point. Keller's Theorem 3.1, Geometry of Synthesis's affine sharing and the NICT abstract all support the flaws above rather than the design.
fixable_flaws.fix: Cite HVM2 as copy-per-call, or drop it. Cite CCSK for what keys buy. Move Keller, Geometry of Synthesis and NICT to the weaknesses section.

fixable_flaws.flaw: The native add and the labels have gaps. Unary add needs b to be held only by the caller. Binary add assumes both lists have the same length, and leaves a top 0 bit when the final carry is 0, which is not canonical if disp's numbers must be. Labels sit only on loaded code nodes, but about a third of fork applications in fib 5 apply runtime-built T2 forks, which carry no label. A jet for a curried function like add only sees the full call two hops away.
fixable_flaws.fix: Specify how unequal lengths and canonical form are handled. Fire a jet on the full application (the fork whose function chain reaches the labelled node). Let labels follow riders that point into labelled code.

fixable_flaws.flaw: 'Simpler' is overstated. Today's net has 14 tags plus Seam in rules.rs, not 13. Riders moves that complexity into frame states (app, hd, tr, stem, fork, rcpt, want, native modes), rider state (pass count, copier mode), and 3-5-agent rules. It also needs pieces not yet written: piles, pulses, labels, buds, demand withdrawal, read marks.
fixable_flaws.fix: Compare at the port level after the fixes above, counting every state and rule the lattice needs.

verdict:
Not workable as written. It survives only as an optimization of today's net, not as a simpler core.

**What holds up:**
- Reading code in place cuts work when a node has few readers at once and few past uses. That is the model's 0.17x.
- Frames that become their values, and receipts that are the frames themselves (K keeps one pointer, not a copy), are good ideas.
- Using the thread as scratch memory works for hand-written routines.

**What breaks as written:**
- Records sit in the read path, so every recursive loop is quadratic. On the design's own benchmark the headline drops to 0.31x work and 0.74x depth of the lazy net, or 0.59x and 1.42x against the net with movement agents. That already fails Step 1's 1.15x depth bar.
- At add 64 1 and fib 8 it does 1.8-2.1x the lazy net's work at 2.8-4.9x its depth.

**Two problems survive any fix that keeps 'code is never copied':**
- Shared nodes are serial, so parallel callers need copies after all.
- Every use of a node shares that node's history. Exact undo without ids then means last-in-first-out coupling that blocks local unwinding (28-36% of fib's garbage records), or heat, or ids.

The lesson: copies are not only for speed. They give each call a private history it can undo alone. Criterion 7 is met only by jets.

Before building Step 1, rerun the model with explicit wire stacks: anchors with side piles, arrival-order reading, two-hop forks, and one reader per node per round. Use add n 1 up to n = 64 and fib up to 8.

My scripts are in /tmp/critic/: contend2.py, pilerounds2.py, compare2.py, buried3.py and latency.py. The inputs are /tmp/critic/scale.txt and /tmp/critic/lazy_scale.txt, from research/linear-nets/target/release/linear-nets. No repo files were changed.

*Automation Opportunity:* a --wires flag in the riders model, plus a scaled calls file next to research/linear-nets/calls.txt, would make quadratic terms show up in every run instead of hiding at add 2 3 sizes.

design: Footprint nets: every rewrite leaves a footprint wired to what it made

fixable_flaws.flaw: The headline trade is false. The design says 'Bennett's clean-up does not work inside the net' (Bennett's clean-up: run forward, copy the answer, run back) and that 'history-free code means a single walker'. Both claims are wrong, because reading does not have to consume. A reader that sits on a wire and passes a value agent without touching its back port follows the design's own no-footprint principle: its output is a twin of what it read, so the twin is the record. I added three rule shapes to the prototype: split a reader at a stem or fork onto the child wires; at a leaf, finish and make a twin leaf; join finished readers into a twin stem or fork. On all 21 compiled calls, forward, then reading, then running every footprint back leaves 0 footprints, a copy equal to the answer, and the rest equal to the loaded net agent for agent. Reading took 3–35 rounds, and 215 for greet "a", whose unary code points are deep. Example: add 2 3 goes from 2,653 footprints to 0 in 896 + 11 + 844 rounds. Run backward, the reader's own rules undo a read exactly, in the same number of rounds, on all 21. The same works with no demand controller at all. research/REVERSIBLE_PIPELINE.md already named this fix ('Bennett's copy needs a reader that does not consume'). Parallel, history-free arithmetic is also standard: [Draper et al. add 'in O(log n) depth', in place](https://arxiv.org/pdf/quant-ph/0406142#page=1).
fixable_flaws.fix: Add the reader: two agent kinds and five rules, no footprints. Restate the trade: zero history costs about twice the time plus a read whose length is set by the answer's depth, and the input (the loaded program) is kept. Then (a, b) -> (a, a+b) with nothing left over is Bennett's second step on compiled disp: copy out a+b, run back, compute b again from (a, a+b) with sub, un-copy b against it with the reader run backward, then run sub back. Untested end to end. During reading, the nodes being read must not be taken back: either finish forward first, or have readers mark the nodes they pass. Probes: /tmp/fpcritic/bennett.py, /tmp/fpcritic/bennett_eager.py, /tmp/fpcritic/reader_inverse.py.

fixable_flaws.flaw: 'Local' is not true as measured. Each round, the prototype's forward schedule works out demand (which work is wanted) by walking the whole net from the root (wanted() in /tmp/fpnet/fpnet.py), and every history figure depends on that walk. On the lattice, demand is local, but a pulse is dropped and re-sent whenever its strand moves (evaluators/rust-ic-strands/README.md, Laziness). That is an unrecorded erasure on a substrate meant to be bijective. The substrate (the lattice run as physics, phys=1) records wanted bits for this reason; this design does not. The paper it cites for allowing such a controller says controllers ['can only compute forwards'](https://www.cs.le.ac.uk/people/iu3/Publications/RC2012-Web.pdf#page=2), so the net plus its controller is not reversible. Measured with no demand (every ready pair fires): all 21 calls still finish, in 1.9–3.9x fewer rounds, but with 1.7–24.6x the footprints. On 12 of the calls, 1.3–5.7x the lazy run's footprints remain even after running back the dead branches.
fixable_flaws.fix: Make demand part of the reversible net. A demand pulse becomes a token that rides its strand instead of being dropped, and each footprint keeps the wanted bits of what it used up, as the substrate does. Or drop demand and rely on the reader's clean-up, which also ends at zero footprints from an eager run, at 1.7–25x the work and peak space. For example, eager fib 3 peaks at 143,612 footprints against 723 loaded agents. Probes: /tmp/fpcritic/eager.py, /tmp/fpcritic/eager_gc.py.

fixable_flaws.flaw: 'Meet, emit, absorb, part and exchange are each bijections on block states' is not shown, and is partly false. (a) A meet between agents 'one strand apart', and an absorb of a product 'within one strand', both forget where the agent sat and how its strand ran. The footprint's kind records only the rule and which products are out, so several block states map to one. The README already says layout does not come back when running back. (b) The move set kept 'unchanged' includes fold, which snaps a U-turn shut and forgets which way it pointed. (c) A deterministic block permutation cannot let 'the drive decide'. Meet and part are inverse maps, so a block holding a ready pair just toggles between them unless agents carry momentum or a direction bit. The cited soft-sphere CA moves because of momentum (its fused particle lasts ['for one step, which then turns back into two particles'](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0806.0127#page=6)). Creutz demons (a small energy counter per site) keep the energy accounts; they do not give a direction. (d) The drive's ε also has to leave the lattice, so commit is not 'the one step that needs an environment'.
fixable_flaws.fix: Pick one physical model. Stochastic: Metropolis or a demon bath with detailed balance, and drop the bijective and quantum claims. Deterministic: give every agent a direction bit (running backward = flipping all of them), emit and absorb products only in fixed relative seats, store the partner's direction in the footprint (about 3 bits), and pair fold with an unfold that keeps the turn's direction. Then count footprint kinds and heat again.

fixable_flaws.flaw: With only meet and part biased, the answer never settles. Emit and absorb are an unbiased coin flip, so every unused product spends about half its time inside its footprint, even after the run ends. I simulated unbiased emit and absorb at the finished answer, without letting any footprint empty. add 2 3's answer, 5, was whole in only 151 of 4,000 samples, about 4%: its 5 forks each flicker, 2^-5. For size [5, 6, 7] it was 12%. If footprints may empty too, the leaves flicker as well and things get worse. The Brownian circuits the design cites finish because a ratchet reads the output; this design has no such step. The cited equilibrium result also needs ['a probability to fork that decreases exponentially as a function of the size of their local memory'](http://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/people/ohad.kammar/publications/bacci-danos-kammar-on-the-statistical-thermodynamics-of-communicating-processes.pdf#page=2). A flat ε per meet, with copying unpriced, does not meet that condition; the 21 runs are fine only because they terminate.
fixable_flaws.fix: Bias emit by a small ε′, paid back by absorb. Make the root reader (N) a ratchet. Price copying rules above other meets, or keep laziness local so forks stay bounded. Probe: /tmp/fpcritic/flicker.py.

fixable_flaws.flaw: The lattice plan does not fit today's lattice, and the proposed first experiment cannot detect this. Partly taken back, the footprints of T·S (the S rule) and D·F (copying a fork) reach 10 wire ends. Q·F (triage on a fork) reaches 8, and T·F, Q·S, D·S and N·F reach 7 (/tmp/fpcritic/arity_check.py). A switchboard holds 8 pairings. Its crowding energy, c·p²/2 with c = 0.5, charges 9 for a single 6-end footprint, more than the substrate's drive ε = 8, so seating footprints is uphill. The experiment keeps the record table, so 'forward unchanged' holds by construction. A partly absorbed record also needs something at the anchor to hold the absorbed product's wires (up to 10 ends), and nothing can be seated there.
fixable_flaws.fix: Test the forward half first, because it is cheaper and can kill the design. On add 1 1, add 2 3, fib 2 and relay_add 13 6, leave an inert footprint agent at every rewrite, with back strands to its products and never undone. Measure clocks, blocked moves and switchboard fill. Only if forward stays within about 1.5x, move on to binary undo with a real footprint agent. That step needs either a higher pairing limit (the README says pairings cost only log bits) or footprints split into chains of agents with at most 3 ports.

fixable_flaws.flaw: Exchange code is unsound next to footprints, undriven, and out of reach of disp. An exchange keeps each agent's back port, so an agent a walker has changed still looks unused to the footprint that made it. In the adder, a column with carry-in 0 keeps its kind on the down sweep but has its pointer reversed. If a footprint made that column, it can absorb it and take the walker's trail as its own rule's wire, which is a state no forward order reaches. Exchanges are not biased ('nothing else is biased'), so the walker diffuses (order n² steps) and does not stay at done. And the adder's bits are agent kinds, while disp's bits are trees (a leaf, or a stem over a leaf): a change of shape, not of kind, so no compiled disp value can be added this way.
fixable_flaws.fix: Have an exchange carry the visited agent's back wire on the walker's trail and hand it back on the return. Otherwise, allow exchanges only on agents whose back port is capped. Make absorb check the product's kind. Bias exchanges. For disp code, use the reader-based Bennett step instead of hand-written walkers.

fixable_flaws.flaw: Without the reader, the heat claims do not hold. The design is Landauer's per-step history made local, which its own cited survey says ['merely delays rather than avoids the thermodynamic cost'](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.20842#page=3). Running back the dead branches clears only 18–31% of footprints, and the rest can only be committed at about one unit per rewrite, which is no better than an irreversible machine. 'Un-copy is free' is not true: each collector-made un-copy (rule 22) leaves a footprint in the answer's causal past. The claim 'floor ≈ 0 when the input is still held' does not apply here, because the net consumes its input. 'One unit of heat per commit' is too low. A footprint holds its kind (rule plus products out, about 9 bits) and where its six wires lead. On a bijective substrate the heat particle must carry all of that, plus the strand paths that are retracted.
fixable_flaws.fix: With the reader, the floor is reachable: run everything back and keep the copy and the input. Price commit as kind bits plus wiring plus strand length. Call un-copy free only when its footprint is later run back.

fixable_flaws.flaw: Two parallelism claims are overstated. (a) 'Each agent has one front port, so ready meetings are disjoint' is false. Collectors meet output ports (rules 22–26), so a duplicator that faces a value and has a collector on each output has three competing meetings. Over the 21 calls there were 268 agent-rounds in which a demanded agent's own meeting and a collector were both ready, and 473 with two collectors on one duplicator. The cited reversibility theorem ([Salikhmetov, Def. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07275#page=4)) covers systems where only principal ports interact, and its no-clash condition fails here. (b) Going back is not 'at least as parallel' per causal step. Each step takes 2 rounds (absorb, then part). With forward not slowed by demand, every run went back in 2.0x its forward rounds (fib 3: 1,505 against 752). The 0.55–1.09x figure is measured against a forward that waits on the demand walk.
fixable_flaws.fix: State how clashes are settled (collector first within a block). It costs nothing measurable: settling clashes at random changed footprint counts by at most 1% (/tmp/fpcritic/noprio.py, /tmp/fpcritic/conflicts.py). Take back in one move every unused product already in the block (the prototype's 'all' mode, 0.28–0.55x), and absorb one at a time only for products that have moved away. Cite the occurrence-net result instead of Salikhmetov.

fixable_flaws.flaw: History can only be cleared all at once, and code is never reused. With a single global drive, the only clean-up is running the whole run back. Peak space is therefore the whole history (8.7–37x the program), and functions are copied rather than reused, so the second half of criterion 6 is not met.
fixable_flaws.fix: Add a local reverse marker: once a reader has copied out a call's result, a token spreads down back wires into that call's footprints and runs them back while the rest of the net keeps going forward. That gives Bennett-style pebbling (clearing history call by call) and returns the function's code instead of leaving copies. Untested.

fixable_flaws.flaw: Three citations are used for claims they do not make. [Hassan, Mackie and Sato](https://www.user.tu-berlin.de/o.runge/tfs/workshops/gtvmt08/Program/paper_38.pdf#page=13) note that agents are consumed, in a remark about sharing, and propose 'to extend interaction nets with data sharing mechanisms'. They say nothing about Bennett, and their direction is the opposite of the design's use. [Keller's Theorem 3.1](https://web.archive.org/web/20240502171700id_/https://scholarship.claremont.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1288&context=hmc_fac_pub#page=8) ('No set of serial modules can be universal for the set of all modules') is about speed-independent circuits and says nothing about history. History-free code can have joins, as the reader does and as Brownian circuits' [CJoin](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.10735#page=9) does. [Lee, Peper et al.](https://www2.nict.go.jp/nano/results/abstract/17_217.html) say arrival order 'may (or may not) destroy' reversibility. Footprints record the order of cause and effect and which side won a clash, not arrival order.
fixable_flaws.fix: Drop or restate these three. Keep Carette et al., but also quote its compute-copy-uncompute section, which argues for the reader fix above.

fixable_flaws.flaw: It is simpler than the substrate, but it is not a new way to use history. In the abstract it is rev.rs's event log (rev.rs: the abstract event-log engine), stored as wired agents with no ids: undo while the products are unused, in any causal order, one record per rewrite. Port counts also grow: every agent gains a back port, Q has 6 ports and T has 5, footprints have up to 10 wire ends, and there are about 150 footprint kinds. The chip (the hardware layout of the lattice) uses cells with at most 3 ports.
fixable_flaws.fix: Present it as rev.rs made local. Keep Pair/Unp if port count matters more than footprint count. Claim new uses of history only once the reader lands.

verdict:
No fatal flaw in the mechanism itself. I attacked the four laws on the abstract net (are they bijections, is 'unused' detected correctly, is causal order kept) and they held. I re-ran the prototype's random-term test: 3,999 of 3,999 terms came back exactly. All 21 compiled calls run. Garbage collection by running back is actually local: freezing the root reader's footprints gives exactly the same state as the prototype's global keep-set on all 21 (/tmp/fpcritic/gc_local.py). As a representation it is sound: rev.rs's history, held as matter, undone one product at a time.

Where it breaks is its conclusions, its physics and its lattice plan.
1. Its central trade is false. A reader that rides wires instead of consuming (three rule shapes, no footprints, an exact inverse) lets Bennett's clean-up run inside the net. All 21 calls end with zero footprints, a correct copy of the answer and the loaded net, with or without demand. History-free and fully parallel can coexist at about twice the time, which is what criteria 6 and 7 ask for and what the design says cannot be done.
2. 'Local' depends on a global demand walk each round; without demand, history grows 1.7–25x.
3. The claimed bijective substrate ignores where agents sit and how strands run, keeps the many-to-one fold, and mixes a Brownian drive with a deterministic permutation. With only meets biased, the answer itself flickers: add 2 3's answer is whole about 4% of the time.
4. Footprints with up to 10 wire ends overfill today's 8-pairing switchboards, and their crowding energy is larger than the drive. The proposed first experiment keeps the record table, so it cannot test this.

Order of work: add the reader first. It turns the history from a log you pay heat to erase into one you spend and get back. Then measure forward clocks with inert footprints as lattice matter, make demand a recorded local signal, and choose stochastic or deterministic physics, biasing emits either way.

The probes are scratch files outside the repo; nothing in the repo was touched or committed: /tmp/fpcritic/{bennett,bennett_eager,reader_inverse,eager,eager_gc,gc_local,conflicts,noprio,flicker,arity_check}.py (they import /tmp/fpnet/fpnet.py).
